title: The Inner Game: Why Your State Matters More Than Your Skills
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: This is Andrea Chiarelli's write-up accompanying a live video conversation with a guest named Deri, a former Bain consultant and startup CFO, on emotional self-regulation under leadership pressure. Deri's own story anchors the piece: years of visible career success at Bain masked mental and physical health he would later rate a three out of ten, and later, as a CFO navigating a brutal company sale with young children at home, that pressure surfaced in a moment of exploding at a call with twenty senior advisers. Chiarelli uses this to introduce the 'above the line / below the line' framework from The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership, distinguishing a calm, curious, open state from a defensive, right-protecting one. The piece argues that self-awareness is trainable through a specific practice — trigger tracking — and that once a team shares this vocabulary, naming a below-the-line moment becomes low-cost rather than embarrassing. It is a short companion piece to a 58-minute video rather than a standalone long-form article, so its scope is intentionally narrow: one story, one framework, one practical tool.
points: Executives can carry severe stress invisibly: Deri rated his mental and physical health a three out of ten during his highest-achieving years at Bain, with none of that pressure visible to observers at the time.

The 'above the line / below the line' framework gives leaders a shared vocabulary for a state shift — calm, curious and open versus defensive and committed to being right — that can be named in the moment rather than only diagnosed afterward.

Deri claims roughly 90% of people recognize the framework instantly, framing the resistant 10% as demonstrating defensiveness rather than disproving the model — a self-reinforcing argument worth reading critically.

The practical entry point is trigger tracking: logging what happened, the thoughts and feelings it produced, the resulting behavior, its impact, and what an above-the-line response would have looked like.
Once a team shares this language, someone can say 'I've dropped below the line, give me a minute' without professional cost, turning individual self-awareness into a team-level asset.
quotes: Six successful, fast-paced years at Bain with rapid promotions came alongside mental and physical health he would later rate at three out of ten.

Then, as CFO of a 60-person boutique going through a brutal sale process, with two children under five at home and twins on the way, he found himself on a call with twenty senior advisers and simply exploded: will you please let me speak?
Above the line, you are calm, curious and open, able to treat a hard week as a story you will tell later. Below it, you are defensive, committed to being right and protecting your position.

Everyone drops below the line several times a day. Deri noted that around 90% of people have a light-bulb moment when they hear this, and that the 10% who object tend to be demonstrating the framework rather than disproving it.
On what to actually do, Deri set out four layers of self-awareness (measure, track, reflect and crack) with trigger tracking as the practical entry point.

Once you develop these skills yourself, the multiplier is the team. If a group shares the language we discussed in our conversation, someone can say I've dropped below the line, give me a minute without it costing them anything, and that shared vulnerability is a real asset.
